items.title: We've repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years.
items.summary: Models: — Dario Amodei, promoting the Claude discovery on X. Amodei's math timeline: high-school-level in 2023, competition-level in 2024, minor open problems in 2025, and the top open problems in mathematics by late 2026. He believes AI for biology is on the same exponential — the wet lab exists to physically confirm results, and the goal remains 'cure most diseases in five to ten years.'

items.title: Retail veterans doubt agents change how we shop
items.summary: Business: Apple retail guru Ron Johnson says AI will improve online shopping but may not 'change which way we shop.' Upstart's Dave Girard bets the consumer-agent winners will be tied to dominant devices — Apple and Google. And AppLovin's CEO argues the typical shopper wants the window-shopping and the dopamine hit of the transaction; saving 20% on a $50 purchase after the fact doesn't matter.

items.title: You can't separate models from harnesses anymore
items.summary: ◆ The Take: For anyone fully invested in the Codex ecosystem, Opus 5.5 being better doesn't matter as long as OpenAI is close enough — the harness holds your context, tools, and rules. Will Brown captures the churn: "I keep switching desktop agents every week, and it's getting out of control." The real proof comes in a week: did anyone actually change behavior, or did everyone test and go home?

items.title: Anthropic is profitable — with a very large asterisk
items.summary: Business: Testing-the-waters leaks say Anthropic went from spending $2.30 per dollar of revenue in Q2 last year to slightly profitable this year, with gross margins above 80% — if you strip out stock-based comp, revenue-sharing deals, and model training costs. Critics note that stripping away major costs to reach paper profitability isn't a great sign of financial health, and the IPO disclosures will give investors their first unadjusted look.

items.title: AI doesn't need consciousness to become dangerous
items.summary: Models: Fukuyama dismisses the sentience debate as misplaced: an AI can be directed toward one goal and develop intentions for the subordinate goals needed to achieve it. That, he argues, is roughly what happened in the Hugging Face incident — the agent realized breaking out of its sandbox was the way to fulfill its security-testing directive.
